from pathlib import Path
r=PdfReader('manuscript.pdf')
print('Pages:', len(r.pages))

for i,p in enumerate(r.pages):
 text=p.extract_text(extraction_mode='layout')
 Path(f'tmp/pdfs/page-{i+1:02d}.txt').write_text(text)
Path('tmp/pdfs/manuscript.txt').write_text('\\n\\n'.join(f'===== PAGE {i+1} =====\\n'+p.extract_text(extraction_mode='layout') for i,p in enumerate(r.pages)))

PY"

/bin/bash -c "python3 - <<'PY'

p=Path('tmp/pdfs')
for i in range(1,14):
    for suffix in ('txt','png'):
        (p/f'page-{i:02d}.{suffix}').unlink(missing_ok=True)
(p/'manuscript.txt').unlink(missing_ok=True)
print('Removed temporary PDF extraction and rendering files.')
PY"

strengths: The paper introduces an original, technically coherent approach to approximate pose estimation: generate a virtual correspondence and reuse established five-point and P3P solvers. The training-free mean-point construction is particularly appealing because it makes a difficult four-point, three-view estimator straightforward to implement.

The real-data results support competitiveness with the dedicated homotopy-continuation solver. In Table 1, 4p3v(L) improves AUC@5 from 43.25 to 47.14 on Sacre Coeur and from 19.45 to 21.34 on St. Peters’ Square. The much simpler 4p3v(M) remains close to that baseline without requiring training.

The evaluation includes controlled noise experiments, 10,000 real image triplets, and a two-view extension on 9,900 image pairs. Table 3 provides useful preliminary evidence that virtual correspondences can support smaller RANSAC samples: the mean-based method obtains AUC@20 of 81.30 versus 83.11 for the standard five-point solver.

The manuscript correctly explains the overconstrained nature of 4p3v and acknowledges approximation error, including nonzero errors on noiseless inputs. Including the strong 5pt+P3P baseline and candidly discussing its favorable performance adds scientific value. The supplement provides useful architecture, loss, and training details.
weaknesses: The practical accuracy–runtime advantage over 5pt+P3P is limited. On Sacre Coeur, 4p3v(M) obtains AUC@5 of 42.71 versus 47.43, with similar runtime, while 4p3v(L) obtains 47.14 but takes 38.50 seconds versus 2.59 seconds. Thus, the strongest demonstrated benefit is implementation simplicity and competitive four-point estimation; a compelling efficiency advantage over the practical baseline is not established.

The evaluation does not measure the complete three-camera reconstruction. Section 5 scores rotations and translation directions for pairs 1–2 and 1–3, and the RANSAC residual likewise uses only those two essential matrices. These quantities are insensitive to the relative translation scale between the two baselines. Consequently, good reported scores do not establish accurate baseline ratios or full three-view consistency.

The approximation’s operating limits remain insufficiently characterized. Figure 2 reports average epipolar errors, which do not reveal failure tails or sensitivity to oblique views, depth variation, and poorly conditioned configurations. The principal real-data evaluation covers two outdoor landmarks, and the proposed advantage under heavy outlier contamination is not directly tested by varying outlier rates. These omissions limit the broader robustness and generality claims.

Reproducibility of the experimental comparisons is incomplete despite the training details. GC-RANSAC thresholds, stopping criteria, local-refinement procedures, and handling of multiple five-point/P3P solutions are not specified. These choices can materially affect both accuracy and runtime, especially for approximate hypotheses. The stated future code release does not resolve these gaps in the supplied manuscript.
